questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes income from wealth?
options: Income includes only wages and salaries; wealth includes all other receipts such as rent, dividends and interest
Income is measured before tax; wealth is the same income measured after tax and transfers
Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock of assets less debts at a point in time
Income is the value of assets a household owns; wealth is what it earns from working each year
questions.explanation: Income, such as wages, rent and dividends, is earned per week or per year. Wealth, or net worth, is the value of assets such as property, shares and super, minus liabilities, measured at a moment in time.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of wealth rather than income?
options: A fortnightly age pension paid to a retired couple by Centrelink
The value of a family's home and shares, less their mortgage
A worker's weekly wage of $1,500 before tax is deducted
The rent received each month from an investment apartment
questions.explanation: Net worth is assets minus liabilities at a point in time. Wages, rent and pensions are all flows of income received over a period.

questions.stem: Why does wealth inequality tend to reinforce income inequality?
options: Assets such as property and shares generate rent, dividends and capital gains for their owners
Wealthy households pay no income tax on their wages, so their after-tax incomes always rise faster
Wealth is counted twice in income statistics, inflating measured income at the top
Households with low wealth are not entitled to receive interest on their bank deposits
questions.explanation: Owning assets brings investment income, and higher incomes allow more saving that builds further wealth. The two kinds of inequality therefore feed each other over time.

questions.stem: Inequality of opportunity refers to differences in:
options: the rates of income tax that people in different tax brackets are required to pay
people's access to education, jobs and services that shape their future outcomes
the incomes that different people earn from their work in the same year
the net worth that different households have built up by retirement
questions.explanation: Inequality of opportunity is about the starting points and chances people have, such as schooling and health care, rather than the outcomes, income and wealth, that are measured afterwards.

questions.stem: A Lorenz curve plots:
options: the cumulative percentage of income against the cumulative percentage of households
the average income of each household against the size of each household
the Gini coefficient of a country against its real GDP per capita over time
the share of income earned by the top 10% of households against the bottom 40% each year
questions.explanation: Households are ranked from poorest to richest along the horizontal axis and the vertical axis shows the share of total income they receive. The diagonal line of equality shows each share of households receiving the same share of income.

questions.stem: On a Lorenz diagram, a curve that bows further away from the line of equality shows:
options: a more equal distribution of income
a higher level of average income
a faster rate of real economic growth
a more unequal distribution of income
questions.explanation: The larger the gap between the Lorenz curve and the diagonal, the smaller the share of income received by lower-ranked households. The curve shows distribution, not the level of income.

questions.stem: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 show about the distribution of a country's income?
options: No households in the population fall below the poverty line
Income and wealth are distributed in exactly the same way
It is perfectly equal, with every household receiving the same income
It is perfectly unequal, with one household receiving all the income
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient runs from 0, perfect equality, to 1, where one household has all the income. Higher values mean greater inequality.

questions.stem: On a Lorenz diagram, the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve is 0.15 and the area beneath the Lorenz curve is 0.35. The Gini coefficient is:
questions.explanation: Gini = area between the line and the curve / total area under the line of equality = 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.35) = 0.30. Dividing by the area under the curve alone gives 0.43, which is a common slip.

questions.stem: The Palma ratio is calculated as:
options: the income share of the top 10% divided by the income share of the bottom 40%
the income share of the top 20% divided by the income share of the bottom 20%
the area between the Lorenz curve and the line of equality, divided by the total area
the median income divided by the income at the OECD poverty line for a household
questions.explanation: The Palma ratio compares the richest tenth with the poorest four-tenths. The top-to-bottom quintile ratio is a different measure, and the area method describes the Gini coefficient.

questions.stem: In a country the top 10% of households receive 26% of income and the bottom 40% receive 20%. The Palma ratio is:
questions.explanation: Palma = top 10% share / bottom 40% share = 26 / 20 = 1.3. Inverting the shares gives 0.77, and subtracting them gives a difference, not a ratio.

questions.stem: One reason economists use the Palma ratio alongside the Gini coefficient is that:
options: the Palma ratio cannot rise above 1, so it is easier to compare across countries
most change in distribution happens at the two ends, which the Palma ratio targets
the Palma ratio measures wealth, while the Gini coefficient only measures income
the Palma ratio takes account of every household, while the Gini uses only the top
questions.explanation: The share of the middle half of households tends to be fairly stable, so the Palma focuses on the top and bottom where shifts occur. The Gini uses the whole distribution and is most sensitive to changes in the middle; both can be applied to income or wealth.

questions.stem: Country A has an income Gini coefficient of 0.32 and Country B has one of 0.45. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Income is distributed more unequally in Country A
Country B must have a higher rate of absolute poverty
Income is distributed more unequally in Country B
Average income must be higher in Country B
questions.explanation: A higher Gini coefficient means a more unequal distribution. It says nothing on its own about average income levels or the number of people in absolute poverty.

questions.stem: In Australia the Gini coefficient for household wealth is much higher than the Gini coefficient for household income. This shows that:
options: wealth is distributed more unevenly than income
income is distributed more unevenly than wealth
wealth inequality has fallen faster than income inequality
the tax-transfer system has no effect on household income
questions.explanation: A higher Gini value means a more unequal distribution, so wealth is more concentrated than income. A single comparison at one time says nothing about trends or about the effect of taxes and transfers.

questions.stem: The Gini coefficient for disposable income in Australia is lower than the Gini coefficient for private (market) income. The main reason is that:
options: disposable income excludes the incomes of the highest-earning households from the statistics
employers pay higher wages to lower-paid workers once their income tax has been deducted
progressive taxes and means-tested transfers redistribute income towards lower-income households
private income includes the value of household assets, which are very unevenly distributed
questions.explanation: Market income is before taxes and government payments. Higher-income earners pay more tax and lower-income households receive more transfers, so disposable income is more evenly spread.

questions.stem: Relative poverty, measured using the OECD poverty line, generally refers to households whose income is below:
options: 50% of average gross weekly earnings for full-time adults
the tax-free threshold for personal income tax in Australia
50% of median equivalised disposable household income
the minimum income needed to buy food and shelter
questions.explanation: The OECD poverty line commonly used in Australia is half the median equivalised disposable household income. Measuring against basic needs describes absolute poverty instead.

questions.stem: Median equivalised disposable household income is $1,200 a week. Using the OECD poverty line, which household is in relative poverty?
options: A household with equivalised disposable income of $1,100 a week
A household with equivalised disposable income of $560 a week
A household with equivalised disposable income of $640 a week
A household with equivalised disposable income of $780 a week
questions.explanation: The poverty line is 50% of the median: 0.5 x $1,200 = $600 a week. Only the household on $560 is below it.

questions.stem: Over a decade the real incomes of the poorest households rise by 10%, while median income rises by 25%. What happens to relative poverty?
options: It is unchanged, because relative poverty depends only on prices
It must fall, because rising median income lowers the poverty line
It may rise, because the poverty line moves up with the median
It must fall, because the poorest households are better off in real terms
questions.explanation: The relative poverty line is half of median income, so it rises 25% while the poorest gain only 10%. More households can fall below it even though their living standards improve in absolute terms.

questions.stem: The cycle of poverty describes how:
options: government payments rise when poverty rises and fall when it falls, smoothing the business cycle
low income limits access to education and health, which lowers future earnings and passes disadvantage on
poverty rises during each economic downturn and falls again during the next expansion
households move above and below the poverty line from one year to the next as their incomes change over time
questions.explanation: Disadvantage in one generation can restrict children's schooling, health and networks, so they also earn less as adults. The movement of poverty with the business cycle is a different idea.

questions.stem: High intergenerational income mobility means that:
options: children's incomes as adults are only weakly linked to their parents' incomes
most people's incomes rise steadily throughout their working lives
workers can move easily between jobs in different parts of the country
parents can transfer their wealth to their children while paying very little tax
questions.explanation: Intergenerational mobility measures how far a person's economic position depends on their family background. Moving between jobs or regions is labour mobility, a separate concept.

questions.stem: A study finds that in Country X the incomes of adult children closely track the incomes of their parents. This most strongly suggests that Country X has:
options: a low Gini coefficient for both income and wealth
a high rate of growth in real GDP per capita
low intergenerational mobility and unequal opportunity
high intergenerational mobility and equal opportunity
questions.explanation: When parents' income strongly predicts their children's, family background shapes outcomes and mobility is low. The finding does not on its own tell us the current Gini coefficient or growth rate.

questions.stem: Graduates earn more on average than people without post-school qualifications, and access to high-quality schooling differs by family income. Which cause of inequality does this describe?
options: Structural economic change
Educational disparities
Asset price inflation
Wealth transfers
questions.explanation: Differences in education lead to differences in skills and earnings, and unequal access to schooling passes these on. Asset price inflation concerns rising values of property and shares.

questions.stem: House prices rise much faster than wages over many years. The most likely effect on inequality is:
options: narrower income gaps as rents fall relative to wages
no effect, since house prices do not count as wealth
wider wealth gaps between home owners and renters
narrower wealth gaps as renters earn higher wages
questions.explanation: Asset price inflation raises the net worth of those who already own property, while renters and first home buyers fall further behind. Homes are the largest part of household wealth in Australia.

questions.stem: Parents give their adult children a large gift to use as a home deposit. This cause of wealth inequality is best described as:
options: an educational disparity
a structural change
a progressive tax
a wealth transfer
questions.explanation: Gifts and inheritances pass wealth between generations, so children of wealthy families start adult life with more assets. Over time this widens gaps between families.

questions.stem: Since the 1980s many routine manufacturing jobs have disappeared in Australia while demand for highly skilled service workers has grown. The most likely effect on income distribution is:
options: a narrower gap, as automation raises the wages of routine workers
no effect, as total employment in the economy stays about the same
a wider gap between the wages of high-skilled and low-skilled workers
a narrower gap, as displaced workers move into higher-paid jobs
questions.explanation: Structural change and technology raise the demand for, and pay of, skilled workers while reducing demand for routine work. This widens the gap between high and low earners even if total employment holds up.

questions.stem: Which government policy change would most likely widen income inequality?
options: Cutting the top marginal income tax rate while freezing welfare payments
Raising income support payments for unemployed and low-income people
Increasing means-tested family payments for low-income households
Raising the tax rate applied to the highest taxable income bracket
questions.explanation: Lower taxes at the top raise high incomes after tax, while frozen payments let low incomes fall behind. The other changes shift disposable income towards lower-income households.

questions.stem: Which factor contributes most directly to inequity in health outcomes in Australia?
options: Universal access to public hospital treatment through Medicare
Higher rates of private health insurance among low-income people
Equal availability of specialists in regional and city areas
Out-of-pocket costs that lead lower-income people to delay or skip care
questions.explanation: Gap fees and costs such as dental care, which Medicare largely does not cover for adults, weigh most heavily on low-income households. Free public hospital care under Medicare reduces inequity rather than causing it.

questions.stem: Which factor contributes to inequity in housing outcomes in Australia?
options: Rising interest rates, which make existing home owners wealthier than renters
A fall in the share of income that low-income renters spend on housing costs
Rising house prices relative to incomes, which lock lower-income households out of ownership
Falling rents relative to incomes, which let renters save for a deposit faster than home owners can
questions.explanation: When prices rise faster than incomes, deposits take longer to save and lower-income households stay renting, often in housing stress. Rising interest rates add to the cost of borrowing rather than raising owners' wealth.

questions.stem: The gender pay gap is:
options: the share of women in the workforce compared with the share of men in the population
the difference between the average earnings of men and women, as a percentage of men's earnings
the difference in pay between a man and a woman doing exactly the same job for the same employer
the difference between the minimum wage and the average wage of full-time female workers
questions.explanation: The gap compares average earnings across the workforce. It is mostly not equal pay for the same work, which has been required by law for decades, but differences in jobs, hours and seniority.

questions.stem: Women are concentrated in industries such as aged care and childcare, which pay less than male-dominated industries such as mining. This contributor to the gender pay gap is called:
options: occupational segregation
the motherhood penalty
the fatherhood premium
a promotion gap at work
questions.explanation: Occupational (industrial) segregation is the clustering of women and men in different industries and jobs with different pay. The motherhood penalty is the loss of earnings after having children.

questions.stem: After the birth of their first child, a mother's earnings fall sharply and stay lower for years, while the father's earnings continue to rise. This illustrates:
options: the cycle of poverty and intergenerational mobility
asset price inflation and wealth transfers
the motherhood penalty and the fatherhood premium
occupational segregation and the glass ceiling
questions.explanation: Mothers often reduce hours or step back from promotion for caring, while fathers' earnings tend to grow. Both widen the gender pay gap over a career.

questions.stem: In a large firm, men and women at each job level are paid the same rates, yet the firm has a large gender pay gap. The most likely explanation is:
options: men hold most of the senior, highest-paid positions in the firm
women are paid less than men for doing the same work at each level
the firm pays all its staff more than the relevant award requires
men and women work the same hours in the same roles at the firm
questions.explanation: If pay is equal at each level, the gap must come from who is at each level: a promotion gap, or vertical segregation. Unequal pay for the same work is ruled out by the scenario.

questions.stem: Which is an argument that some economic inequality can benefit the economy?
options: Inequality lowers the share of income spent on consumption, raising total demand
Inequality raises intergenerational mobility by giving the poor more opportunity
Inequality reduces government spending on welfare by raising average incomes
Differences in reward give people incentives to work, train and take business risks
questions.explanation: Higher rewards for skill and enterprise encourage effort and innovation. High inequality, however, tends to reduce mobility and can weaken demand, so the other claims are wrong.

questions.stem: Which is a negative social effect of high inequality?
options: Greater incentive for low-income workers to gain new skills and change jobs
Higher rates of saving across all households, lowering interest rates
Lower demand for government services such as public health care, education and social housing
Social exclusion, as low-income people cannot take part in normal community activities
questions.explanation: Social exclusion means being shut out of activities most people take for granted, which can harm health, education and social cohesion. Inequality usually raises, rather than lowers, demand for public support.

questions.stem: Low-income households spend a larger share of any extra income than high-income households do. Which conclusion follows?
options: Redistributing income towards high-income households will raise total consumption
Inequality has no effect on aggregate demand, as total income is unchanged
Low-income households save more of their extra income than the wealthy do
Redistributing income towards low-income households may raise total consumption
questions.explanation: Low-income households have a higher marginal propensity to consume, so moving income to them tends to lift spending. This is one way high inequality can weaken aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Which best describes the long-term trend in inequality in Australia since the 1980s?
options: Income inequality has fallen steadily as wages grew fastest at the bottom of the scale
Wealth inequality has fallen as home ownership rose among young adults
Income and wealth inequality have both remained exactly constant throughout
Income inequality has risen moderately and wealth inequality has grown with house prices
questions.explanation: Income inequality rose moderately from the 1980s, and rising property prices have widened gaps in wealth, especially between owners and non-owners. Home ownership among young adults has fallen, not risen.

questions.stem: A scatterplot of OECD countries shows that countries with higher income Gini coefficients tend to have lower intergenerational mobility. The best interpretation is:
options: higher inequality causes lower mobility in every single country, so the causal link is proven by the plot
the two measures are unrelated, because each country's data point is in a different place
more unequal countries have more mobility, because the points slope upwards to the right
more unequal countries tend to have less mobility, though the plot alone does not prove causation
questions.explanation: The pattern is a negative relationship between inequality and mobility, sometimes called the Great Gatsby curve. A scatterplot shows correlation; other factors may explain both, so causation needs more evidence.

questions.stem: A table shows that the lowest income quintile receives 7% of household income and the highest quintile receives 42%. The ratio of the top quintile's share to the bottom quintile's share is:
questions.explanation: The ratio is 42 / 7 = 6, so the top fifth of households receives six times the share of the bottom fifth. 35 is the difference in percentage points, not a ratio.
